title: Bright red rectal bleeding in a 42-year-old engineer
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 42-year-old electronics engineer in general practice. He has had 2 days of painless bright red blood on the toilet paper, a feeling of fullness after opening his bowels, years of on-and-off constipation and a low-fibre diet. He is worried about bowel cancer because his father died of cancer. The candidate then interprets a proctoscopy report and blood tests, recognises grade I internal haemorrhoids, and plans conservative treatment, referral for colonoscopy and safety netting.
focus: Rectal bleeding in general practice: telling haemorrhoids apart from the differentials that matter, assessing colorectal cancer risk, and planning conservative treatment and colonoscopy
presentation: Bright red blood on the toilet paper
stem: You are a medical student on your general practice rotation. Peter, a 42-year-old electronics engineer, has come to see the GP because he has noticed bleeding from his back passage. Your supervising GP has asked you to see him first. A practice nurse is available to act as a chaperone.
tasks: Take a focused history from Peter and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Peter's proctoscopy report and his blood test results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Peter, a 42-year-old electronics engineer. You are well, a little embarrassed and clearly worried. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've noticed some blood when I go to the toilet, and I'm a bit worried about it."

The bleeding (give only when asked):

  • The blood is coming from your bottom (anus). It started suddenly 2 days ago, and you can't think of anything that set it off.
  • It is a small amount of bright red blood on the toilet paper when you wipe after a bowel motion.
  • It is not mixed in with the poo and you have not seen it in the toilet bowl.
  • It doesn't hurt.
  • It has been the same since it started. Nothing makes it better or worse.
  • You have no idea why it is happening.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • You get a feeling of fullness in your back passage after a bowel motion.
  • You have had constipation on and off for years. It has not changed recently.
  • If asked about straining: "Not really."

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • A lump coming out of your bottom, or anything you have to push back in.
  • Mucus or discharge, or itching around your bottom.
  • Pain when opening your bowels, or a painful lump at your bottom.
  • Any recent change in how often you go or what your poo is like, diarrhoea, or poo that is black or tarry.
  • A constant urge to go again with nothing coming out.
  • Tummy pain, weight loss, tiredness, breathlessness or dizziness.
  • Waking at night to open your bowels, or having to rush to the toilet.
  • Sore joints, red or painful eyes, skin rashes or mouth ulcers.
  • Fevers or night sweats.
  • Blood-thinning tablets, previous bleeding problems, a previous colonoscopy, or liver problems.
  • Anyone in the family with bowel cancer or bowel polyps.

Impact: it hasn't really affected your life, apart from the worry.

Past medical history: vasectomy at 38. Tennis elbow in your 20s.

Medications: Panadol or Nurofen now and then for headaches. Nothing else.

Allergies: peanuts. No medicine allergies.

Family history:

  • Mother: hysterectomy at 52, high blood pressure.
  • Father: died of testicular cancer at 56.
  • Your brothers and sisters are well.

Social history:

  • Social smoker: a few cigarettes when you are stressed.
  • Alcohol: a glass of red wine on weeknights and a bit more on weekends. If asked to put a number on it: "a couple of extra glasses on Friday and Saturday".
  • Electronics engineer.
  • You go cycling with your children on weekends.
  • Dinner is cooked at home, but at work you eat a lot of fast food and not much fibre.
  • You live with your wife and two children and feel well supported.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I'm not sure why it's happening."
  • Concern: "I'm worried it could be bowel cancer." If asked why: "Dad died of cancer, so I'm very worried."
  • Expectation: you want to know whether it is anything serious.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Could this be bowel cancer? My dad died of cancer."

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: well, comfortable, not pale. Weight 82 kg, height 178 cm, BMI 26 (overweight range).
  • Observations: HR 74 regular, BP 128/80, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C.
  • Hands and eyes: no koilonychia, palmar pallor, clubbing or palmar erythema. Conjunctivae pink. No scleral icterus.
  • Abdomen: not distended. Soft and non-tender. No masses. No hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, spider naevi or caput medusae. Bowel sounds normal.
  • Lymph nodes: no inguinal or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
  • Perianal inspection (with consent and a chaperone, left lateral position): normal skin. No external haemorrhoids, skin tags, fissure, fistula opening or excoriation. Nothing prolapses when he bears down.
  • Digital rectal examination: normal anal tone, not tender. No masses felt. Smooth, normal-sized prostate. Soft brown stool on the glove, with no blood or melaena.
  • Proctoscopy (if the candidate offers or recommends it): "Your supervising GP will do this at the end of the consultation. The report is given in Part 2."

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Peter's identity and gains consent.
Uses plain language, puts him at ease about an embarrassing topic, and acknowledges his worry about cancer and his father's death with empathy, without false reassurance.
History
Characterises the bleeding:

kids.x: Colour and amount: a small amount of bright red blood.
Where the blood is: on the toilet paper after wiping only, not in the bowl and not mixed with the stool.
Onset and course: sudden onset 2 days ago, no trigger, unchanged since, nothing makes it better or worse.
Pain: painless, with no pain on opening his bowels.

check.x: Asks about symptoms of haemorrhoids: a feeling of fullness after a bowel motion (present), straining, a lump or prolapse, mucus discharge and itch (absent).
check.d: Award if the fullness is elicited and at least two of the others are asked.

check.x: Takes the bowel habit: chronic intermittent constipation for years, with no recent change in frequency or consistency.
Screens for features of colorectal cancer:

kids.x: Change in bowel habit, tenesmus, blood mixed with the stool, or dark or black stools.
Weight loss, tiredness or symptoms of anaemia (breathlessness, dizziness), and abdominal pain.
Family history of bowel cancer or polyps (none).

check.x: Screens for inflammatory bowel disease: diarrhoea, mucus, urgency or nocturnal bowel motions, and extra-intestinal features (joints, eyes, skin, mouth ulcers).
check.d: Award for bowel symptoms plus at least one extra-intestinal feature.

check.x: Screens for anal fissure and external or thrombosed haemorrhoids: severe pain during or after defaecation, or a painful perianal lump.
Takes the past medical history: vasectomy at 38, tennis elbow in his 20s; no previous bleeding, colonoscopy or liver disease.
Takes a medication and allergy history, asking specifically about anticoagulants and antiplatelets: occasional Panadol or Nurofen for headaches only; peanut allergy.
Takes a family history: mother had a hysterectomy at 52 and has hypertension, father died of testicular cancer at 56, siblings well.

Takes a social history: social smoker, quantifies alcohol (a glass of red on weeknights and more on weekends), low-fibre fast food at work, cycles with his children, electronics engineer, lives with his wife and two children.
check.d: Award for smoking, alcohol, diet and home situation.

check.x: Explores impact and his ideas, concerns and expectations: little impact apart from worry, unsure of the cause, worried about bowel cancer because his father died of cancer, wants to know if it is serious.
Examination
Asks for vital signs and BMI: observations normal; BMI 26 (overweight).
Looks for signs of anaemia: conjunctival and palmar pallor, koilonychia.
Examines the abdomen for tenderness, masses and hepatomegaly, looks for signs of chronic liver disease, and checks the inguinal nodes.
Explains the perianal and rectal examination, gains specific consent and offers a chaperone.
Inspects the perianal area at rest and on bearing down: no external haemorrhoids, skin tags, fissure, fistula or prolapse.
Performs a digital rectal examination: tone, tenderness, masses, prostate, and the glove for blood or melaena.
Offers or recommends proctoscopy, stating that internal haemorrhoids usually cannot be felt on rectal examination.
check.d: Award for offering or recommending proctoscopy; the explanation is desirable but not required.

check.x: Interpretation

Interprets the proctoscopy: grade I internal haemorrhoids at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock with fresh blood on one cushion and no prolapse on straining; no fissure; normal lower rectal mucosa with no mass, polyp or proctitis.
States that proctoscopy sees only the anal canal and lower rectum, so finding haemorrhoids does not exclude a second cause higher in the bowel.
Interprets the bloods: normal haemoglobin, MCV and ferritin (no anaemia or iron deficiency to suggest chronic blood loss) and normal CRP (against active inflammation such as IBD).

Gives grade I internal haemorrhoids as the most likely diagnosis and justifies it: painless bright red blood on the paper after wiping, fullness after defaecation, chronic constipation, low-fibre diet, no systemic features or change in bowel habit, and the proctoscopy.
Gives differentials, each with a feature for or against:

kids.x: Colorectal (colon or rectal) cancer: age 42, low-fibre diet, smoking and alcohol, and fullness after defaecation; against: no change in bowel habit or weight loss, normal rectal examination, haemoglobin and ferritin.
Anal fissure and external haemorrhoids: against: painless, no lump, normal perianal inspection.
Inflammatory bowel disease: against: no diarrhoea, mucus or extra-intestinal features, and a normal CRP.

check.x: Management
Explains haemorrhoids in plain words: swollen cushions of blood vessels just inside the back passage that bleed when hard stool passes over them; very common and treatable.
Answers his question about the cause by naming his own risk factors: a low-fibre diet and chronic constipation (he denies significant straining, but hard stool and straining are the mechanism).
Starts conservative treatment:

kids.x: More dietary fibre (fruit, vegetables, wholegrains) and fluids, with a bulk-forming fibre supplement such as psyllium.

Toilet habits: go when he feels the urge, avoid straining and long periods sitting on the toilet, avoid constipating medicines such as codeine, and prefer paracetamol over NSAIDs (ibuprofen) while he is bleeding.
A topical haemorrhoid preparation (local anaesthetic with or without a corticosteroid) for symptoms, as a short course only.
kids.d: Optional for bleeding alone; award if offered with the short-course caution.

check.x: Refers for colonoscopy (gastroenterologist or colorectal surgeon), explaining that proctoscopy cannot clear the bowel above and that at his age a second cause should be excluded.
Mentions rubber band ligation if bleeding persists.
Safety netting

Tells him to see the GP sooner if the bleeding gets heavier or does not settle, the blood is mixed in his poo or the poo turns dark or black, his bowel habit changes, or he loses weight, feels tired or breathless, or gets tummy pain or a painful lump at his bottom.
check.d: Award for at least four red flags in plain words.

check.x: Tells him to go to the ED, or call 000, if he passes a large amount of blood or clots, or feels faint or dizzy.

Addresses his worry about cancer honestly: the findings and normal bloods are reassuring, his father's testicular cancer does not increase his own bowel cancer risk, and the colonoscopy will check for anything else; does not promise that it is not cancer.
Arranges follow-up: GP review in a few weeks to check the bleeding and his response to treatment, confirms the colonoscopy referral and appointment, and offers written information.

part2.lead: Your supervising GP performed a proctoscopy at the end of the consultation, and the blood tests requested at the first visit came back two days later. Peter is back for his results. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Ask "Why have I got these?" and "Do I really need a camera test?" during the management answer, and ask "So you're saying it's not cancer?" during the final answer.

You are relieved by a clear, honest explanation. If the candidate uses jargon such as "proctoscopy", "haemorrhoids" or "colonoscopy" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Proctoscopy report
handover.result:
Procedure: rigid proctoscopy in the practice, left lateral position, with a chaperone. Performed by the supervising GP.

Clinical details: 42-year-old man with 2 days of painless bright red blood on the toilet paper, a feeling of fullness after defaecation and long-standing intermittent constipation. Normal perianal inspection and digital rectal examination.

Findings:

  • Anal canal: three enlarged, congested vascular cushions above the dentate line at the 3, 7 and 11 o'clock positions (lithotomy convention; left lateral, right posterior and right anterior). A spot of fresh blood on the cushion at 3 o'clock. No prolapse of the cushions on straining. No fissure, ulcer or fistula opening.
  • Lower rectum (seen to about 8 cm): pink, healthy mucosa with a normal vascular pattern. No mass, polyp, ulceration or proctitis.

Conclusion: grade I internal haemorrhoids, the likely source of bleeding. The bowel above the reach of the proctoscope has not been examined.
handover.model:
• Read: enlarged internal cushions at the three classic positions (3, 7 and 11 o'clock) above the dentate line, one with fresh blood, and no prolapse on straining: grade I internal haemorrhoids. No fissure. Normal lower rectal mucosa with no mass, polyp or proctitis.
  • For Peter: this fits his painless bright red blood on the paper after wiping and the fullness after defaecation, with constipation and a low-fibre diet behind it. They sit above the dentate line, which is why they are painless; they could not be felt on rectal examination because soft vascular cushions collapse under the finger.
  • What it changes: it supports conservative treatment of the haemorrhoids. It does not clear the rest of the bowel. Haemorrhoids are common and can coexist with a polyp or cancer higher up, so at 42 with new rectal bleeding he should be referred for colonoscopy (optimal care pathway), and bleeding that persists despite treatment also needs colonoscopy.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.model:
• Read: haemoglobin 151 and MCV 89 are normal; white cells and platelets normal. Ferritin 142, iron and transferrin saturation normal. CRP 2.
  • For Peter: no anaemia and no iron deficiency, so there is no sign of the slow, hidden blood loss a bowel cancer can cause. A normal CRP argues against active inflammation such as inflammatory bowel disease. A normal platelet count makes a bleeding tendency unlikely (no clotting tests are needed for this picture).
  • What it changes: the results are reassuring and support a non-urgent plan, but normal bloods do not exclude a polyp or early cancer. Iron deficiency anaemia would have made colonoscopy urgent.

ask: You are now presenting Peter to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Peter, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Peter is with you. Explain to him what is causing his bleeding and outline your management now, here in general practice.
Before Peter goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student; Peter, 42, electronics engineer.
  • Situation: 2 days of painless bright red rectal bleeding at presentation (now about 4 days); proctoscopy shows grade I internal haemorrhoids.
  • Background: a small amount on the paper after wiping, not in the bowl or mixed with stool; fullness after defaecation; years of intermittent constipation, low-fibre diet. No change in bowel habit, weight loss or anaemia symptoms. No family history of bowel cancer (father died of testicular cancer). Social smoker, regular wine.
  • Assessment: normal obs; BMI 26; normal abdomen, perianal inspection and DRE. Proctoscopy: grade I internal haemorrhoids, normal lower rectum, bowel above not seen. Hb, ferritin and CRP normal.
  • Recommendation: fibre, fluids and toilet habits; colonoscopy referral; review in a few weeks.

Most likely: grade I internal haemorrhoids. Painless bright red blood on the paper after wiping, fullness after defaecation, chronic constipation and a low-fibre diet, no systemic features or change in bowel habit. Proctoscopy: cushions at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock with fresh blood and no prolapse.

  • Colon or rectal cancer: for: age 42, low fibre, smoking, alcohol, fullness. Against: stable bowel habit, no weight loss, normal DRE, Hb and ferritin. Not excluded above the reach of the proctoscope.
  • Anal fissure: against: painless, no fissure seen.
  • External haemorrhoids: against: no lump, pain or itch; normal inspection.
  • IBD: against: no diarrhoea, mucus or extra-intestinal features; CRP normal.

1. Explain haemorrhoids in plain words and their cause (low fibre, constipation).
  2. Conservative treatment: more dietary fibre and fluids, a bulk-forming supplement such as psyllium, go when he has the urge, no straining or long sitting on the toilet, avoid constipating medicines such as codeine, and prefer paracetamol over NSAIDs (ibuprofen) while he is bleeding. A short course of a topical preparation if he has symptoms.
  3. Colonoscopy referral to gastroenterology or colorectal surgery: proctoscopy cannot clear the bowel above, and at his age a second cause should be excluded.
  4. If bleeding persists: rubber band ligation.

• See the GP sooner if the bleeding gets heavier or doesn't settle, blood is mixed in the poo or the poo is dark or black, his bowel habit changes, he loses weight, feels tired or breathless, or gets tummy pain or a painful lump at his bottom.
  • Go to the ED or call 000 for heavy bleeding or clots, or if he feels faint or dizzy.
  • Reassure honestly: his father's testicular cancer does not raise his bowel cancer risk; the colonoscopy checks for anything else.
  • Follow-up: GP review in a few weeks (bleeding, bowel habit, diet), the colonoscopy appointment, and written information.

ddx.for: Painless bright red blood on the paper after wiping, fullness after defaecation, chronic constipation and a low-fibre diet, with bleeding internal cushions and no prolapse on proctoscopy.
New rectal bleeding at 42 with a low-fibre diet, smoking and regular alcohol.
ddx.against: No change in bowel habit, weight loss, abdominal pain or anaemia symptoms, with a normal haemoglobin and ferritin.

ddx.for: A feeling of fullness after defaecation with new bright red bleeding.
ddx.against: Normal digital rectal examination and normal lower rectal mucosa on proctoscopy, with no tenesmus.

ddx.for: Bright red blood on the paper in a man with chronic constipation.
ddx.against: Painless bleeding with no pain on defaecation, and no fissure on inspection or proctoscopy.
No perianal lump, pain or itch, and a normal perianal inspection.

ddx.dx: Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative proctitis or colitis)
ddx.for: Rectal bleeding in a working-age adult.
ddx.against: No diarrhoea, mucus, urgency, nocturnal symptoms or extra-intestinal features, a normal rectal mucosa and a normal CRP.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart. Give the observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1, give findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The candidate should explain the rectal examination, gain consent and offer a chaperone before you give the perianal and DRE findings. If the candidate offers proctoscopy, say the supervising GP will do it and the report comes in Part 2. If they ask for blood tests, say they have been requested. In Part 2, hand over both results, then ask the four questions in order. Peter asks two of his questions during the management answer and the third ("So you're saying it's not cancer?") during the final answer.

Credit a candidate who screens in the history for each of the six differentials: internal haemorrhoids, colon cancer, rectal cancer, anal fissure, external haemorrhoids and IBD.

A high-performing candidate:

  • pins down where the blood is (on the paper, not mixed with the stool), its colour and that it is painless;
  • takes the bowel habit and screens systematically for cancer, IBD, fissure and external haemorrhoid features, and picks up the low-fibre diet and constipation;
  • asks specifically about a family history of bowel cancer and recognises that his father's testicular cancer does not affect his bowel cancer risk;
  • examines with consent and a chaperone, including perianal inspection and DRE;
  • in Part 2, reads grade I internal haemorrhoids but states that proctoscopy does not clear the bowel above;
  • starts fibre, fluids and toilet advice, refers for colonoscopy, answers his worry honestly and gives clear red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history without locating the blood or screening for cancer features. They may skip consent for the DRE, stop at "it's just haemorrhoids" without considering a second cause, or promise him it is not cancer. Ordering an iFOBT to investigate visible bleeding is not appropriate.
explain:
Diagnosis

Peter most likely has grade I internal haemorrhoids. Small amounts of painless, bright red blood on the toilet paper after wiping, not mixed with the stool, point to a source in the anal canal. A sense of fullness after defaecation, years of intermittent constipation and a low-fibre diet fit. He has no systemic features and no change in bowel habit. The proctoscopy confirms congested internal cushions at the classic 3, 7 and 11 o'clock positions, one with fresh blood, and no prolapse.

Haemorrhoids

Haemorrhoids are cushions of vascular tissue in the anal canal. Internal haemorrhoids lie above the dentate line, where there are no somatic pain fibres, so they are painless. They typically bleed bright red blood after defaecation and may cause fullness, mucus discharge or prolapse. They usually cannot be felt on DRE, because soft vascular cushions collapse under the finger, and are seen on proctoscopy. They are graded by prolapse:

  • Grade I: bleed but do not prolapse.
  • Grade II: prolapse on straining and go back by themselves.
  • Grade III: prolapse and need to be pushed back.
  • Grade IV: prolapsed and cannot be pushed back.

External haemorrhoids lie below the dentate line. They cause a lump and itch, and severe pain when thrombosed. Risk factors are increasing age, a low-fibre diet, chronic constipation and straining, obesity, pregnancy and portal hypertension.

Differentials that matter

  • Colon and rectal cancer: rectal bleeding is often benign, but consider malignancy when there are risk factors or systemic symptoms. Ask about a change in bowel habit, blood mixed with the stool or dark blood, tenesmus or a feeling of incomplete emptying, weight loss, fatigue and anaemia, abdominal pain, and a family history of bowel cancer or polyps. Peter's fullness after defaecation is typical of haemorrhoids, but a rectal tumour can cause a similar feeling, which is another reason for the DRE. His father's testicular cancer does not raise his own bowel cancer risk, but his worry is real and needs addressing.
  • Anal fissure: bright red blood with severe, sharp pain during and after defaecation, usually after passing a hard stool. A fissure is usually seen in the posterior midline.
  • External or thrombosed haemorrhoids: a painful or itchy perianal lump.
  • Inflammatory bowel disease: bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency, nocturnal symptoms, tenesmus and extra-intestinal features, often with a raised CRP.

Interpreting the results

  • Proctoscopy: confirms grade I internal haemorrhoids and a normal lower rectum. It sees only the anal canal and lower rectum, so it cannot exclude a polyp or cancer higher up. Haemorrhoids are common, and finding them does not prove they are the only cause.
  • Bloods: no anaemia or iron deficiency, so there is no sign of chronic hidden blood loss, and a normal CRP argues against active IBD. Iron deficiency anaemia would make investigation more urgent.

Management

  • Examine everyone with rectal bleeding or pain: perianal inspection and DRE with consent and a chaperone, and proctoscopy where available.
  • Conservative treatment (eTG): more dietary fibre and fluids, a bulk-forming laxative such as psyllium, no straining or prolonged sitting on the toilet, and avoiding constipating drugs. Topical preparations containing a local anaesthetic and/or a corticosteroid can ease symptoms; corticosteroid preparations are for short-term use only.
  • Persistent bleeding: haemorrhoids that keep bleeding despite conservative measures can be treated with rubber band ligation. Haemorrhoidectomy is kept for larger, prolapsing or refractory haemorrhoids.
  • Colonoscopy: Cancer Council Australia's optimal care pathway recommends that people with rectal bleeding, including those under 50, are referred for colonoscopy rather than iFOBT; referral now is appropriate given his age, the new bleeding and his worry. Bleeding that persists despite conservative measures also needs colonoscopy.
  • Screening versus investigation: bowel bleeding can be hidden (occult). The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program offers a free immunochemical faecal occult blood test (iFOBT) every 2 years to people aged 45 to 74; at 45–49 people request their first kit through the NBCSP rather than being sent one automatically. This is a screening test for people without symptoms. A screening iFOBT is not the test for visible bleeding: visible rectal bleeding needs clinical assessment and, where indicated, colonoscopy. After Peter's colonoscopy, the specialist will advise when screening should resume.
  • Lifestyle: brief smoking cessation advice, and alcohol within the NHMRC guideline of no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day. A glass of red wine is often more than one standard drink.

Safety netting

He should see the GP sooner if:

  • the bleeding becomes heavier or persists;
  • the blood is mixed with the stool or the stool turns dark or black;
  • his bowel habit changes;
  • he loses weight, feels tired or breathless, or develops abdominal pain or a painful perianal lump.

Heavy bleeding, clots or feeling faint mean the ED or 000. Arrange a GP review in a few weeks to check his response to treatment, and confirm the colonoscopy appointment.
points: Painless bright red blood on the toilet paper after wiping, not mixed with the stool, points to an anal canal source, most often internal haemorrhoids.

Screen every patient with rectal bleeding for features of colorectal cancer (change in bowel habit, blood mixed with stool, tenesmus, weight loss, anaemia, family history of bowel cancer), and for IBD, fissure and external haemorrhoids.
Examine everyone with rectal bleeding or pain: perianal inspection and DRE with consent and a chaperone, plus proctoscopy. Internal haemorrhoids are painless and usually cannot be felt.

Finding haemorrhoids does not clear the bowel above: refer adults with new rectal bleeding, including those under 50, for colonoscopy, and investigate bleeding that persists despite conservative treatment.

Conservative treatment is more fibre and fluids, a bulk-forming laxative and no straining; rubber band ligation treats persistent bleeding. Risk factors are age, low fibre, constipation and straining, obesity, pregnancy and portal hypertension.
The iFOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms (free every 2 years from 45 to 74 through the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program), not a test for visible bleeding.
